scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
The Neo survey is coming — but not yet, and the order matters. A survey can only measure the questions you already know to ask. Fielded too early, it measures our assumptions instead of the market. That's why the qualitative phase runs first: focus groups give us the buyers' own vocabulary, the feature reactions we should turn into scaled questions, and the price expectations that tell us where to center the willingness-to-pay items.

A professional moderator named Renee ran four hour-long groups (this session ran about a quarter-hour over — engaged groups do) against the moderator's guide we built — Orange County, San Diego, Los Angeles, and the Inland Empire. The transcripts are in. I've asked Marcus to route you the **Inland Empire session** for a full analyst's read.

Work backward from the decision, as always: Neo needs a competitive set confirmed by real buyers, a feature specification the room actually argued for, and price expectations grounded in what people said they would pay — not what the trade press says they should. Marcus's memo in your **Inbox** has the transcript attached, the round 4 articles are condensed under **Resources** if you want to cross-reference, and the **Guides** button has our method for mining a transcript. Take your time with it; a transcript rewards a second pass.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Neo focus groups are done — your session is attached
inbox.body:
The fieldwork firm delivered. Renee ran all four Neo groups last week, and she's as good as advertised — watch how she handles the loud guy in your session, because someday that skill will save one of your projects.

Dana wants an analyst's read of the raw material before the firm's topline report lands, and you've drawn **Session 3 of 4 — Inland Empire homeowners, n = 8**. Full transcript attached. Three extractions, same shape as round 4:

1. **Competitive set.** Which companies do these buyers actually name and cross-shop? Count the mentions, but also weigh how people talk — a brand named with respect, a brand the room reclassifies into a different category, and a brand nobody mentions at all are three different competitive facts.
2. **Feature reactions.** Listen for intensity. "Non-negotiable" is a different data point than a shrug, even though both are one mention. The silent-writing exercise and the closing one-thing-perfect round are the cleanest reads in the session.
3. **Price expectations.** Renee ran the written price-ladder exercise from our guide — every participant wrote three numbers before anyone spoke: where the price feels like a bargain, where it starts getting expensive, and where it's too expensive to consider. Find the middle of the room on each rung — medians, not means — and notice what the participants themselves anchored on.

One caution: this is eight people in one metro. It generates hypotheses for the survey; it doesn't size anything. But within that limit, this room was unusually clear about what it wants.

The round 4 articles are condensed in Resources if you want to check the qual against the secondary read. Findings by Thursday — Dana's syncing with Neo on Friday.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Focus Group Transcript — Neo Smart Living Concept Study, Session 3 of 4 (Inland Empire homeowners, n = 8)
attachments.body:
**Session 3 of 4 — Inland Empire homeowners, n = 8**

*Moderator: Renee (Fieldwork West). Participants identified by first name only, ages in parentheses: Marisol (41), Derek (55), Priya (38), Tom (64), Alicia (32), Greg (47), Wendy (59), Sam (36). Recorded and transcribed with participant consent; timestamps approximate.*

---

[00:00] RENEE: Good evening, everybody, and thank you for giving us your Tuesday. My name is Renee, and I moderate discussions like this for a living — which means my job tonight is to ask questions and then get out of your way. Ground rules: there are no wrong answers, only opinions. I want to hear from all eight of you, and if you disagree with someone, say so — disagreement is data. We're recording, first names only, and nothing you say leaves this room with your name on it. Tonight we're talking about backyard structures — finished studios, offices, that sort of thing. Let's go around: first name, how long you've owned your home, and the honest state of your backyard.

MARISOL: Marisol. Eleven years in Rancho Cucamonga. The backyard is a patio set we never sit on and a lawn my husband is at war with.

[laughter]

DEREK: Derek. Twenty-two years in Riverside. I've done most of the work on my place myself — deck, pergola, irrigation — and I've been pricing these backyard studio things for about a year, so fair warning, I have opinions.

RENEE: We'll put the opinions to work, Derek.

PRIYA: Priya. Six years in Corona. The backyard is nice and completely unused. I've been working from my kitchen table since 2020 and I am at the end of my rope.

TOM: Tom. Thirty-one years in Redlands, retired teacher. The yard is mostly citrus trees. I'm here because my wife wants what she calls a garden room, and I want to know what these things actually cost.

[laughter]

ALICIA: Alicia. Fontana, bought in 2023. I teach yoga, and I've been dreaming about a home studio since the day escrow closed.

GREG: Greg, Ontario, nine years. Backyard status: trampoline, dead grass, potential.

WENDY: Wendy, Moreno Valley, sixteen years. Empty nest as of June, so we're rethinking the whole property.

SAM: Sam, Upland, four years. Graphic designer, working out of a spare corner of the bedroom. The dog has a better office than I do.

[00:07] RENEE: Wonderful. Let's start wide. When I say "a small finished building for your backyard — a studio, not a shed" — what comes to mind? What have you seen, heard of, maybe looked into?

DEREK: The Autonomous WorkPod. Their ads are everywhere, and the product's legit — a buddy of mine in Corona has one. Insulated out of the box, power comes in on one cable, and he had the pro install crew done in a day. I've had it in my spreadsheet for a year.

PRIYA: Same one for me. There's a WorkPod two doors down from us — a woman on my street uses hers as an office, and I have coveted it for two years.

SAM: I've gone deep on Studio Home's website. They have this configurator — sizes, doors, windows, colors — and the price moves every time you click. Kind of addictive, honestly. It starts around eighteen and climbs fast, and the installation is a separate conversation.

WENDY: My neighbors put in a Modern Shed two summers ago. Custom — it matches their house, same siding, same trim. It looks like it grew there. But it was a whole design process with a consultant, no price list anywhere, and they had to coordinate the installer themselves. Beautiful, though.

GREG: I'll be honest, the thing that caught my eye online was one of those expandable ones — Elite Nest? Four hundred square feet for seventeen grand, kitchen, bathroom, the works. Made these studio prices look insane.

DEREK: That's not the same product, Greg. Kitchen and a bathroom means it's a dwelling — sewer hookup, foundation, permits, the whole inspection carnival. That's a tiny home you're installing, not a studio you're buying.

TOM: My neighbor went down that road — one of those fold-out BOXABL casitas, the famous one. Lovely unit. By the time the site work, utilities, and permits were done it was a hundred and fifty grand and most of a year. Different animal entirely.

RENEE: Tom, I want to flag the phrase — a purchase versus a project. Does that line ring true for the rest of you?

MARISOL: Completely. The entire appeal is skipping the contractor circus. If it needs permits and a foundation crew, I'm out.

ALICIA: Same. I want it delivered, working, done. Ideally before summer.

GREG: Fine, I'm converted. I need an office, not a second house.

[00:14] RENEE: So imagine you're actually shopping next month. Who's on your short list? Just names.

PRIYA: The WorkPod, and then whoever can convince me they're as good as the WorkPod for less.

[laughter]

SAM: Studio Home, if I can ever stop playing with the configurator. And the WorkPod to compare against.

GREG: WorkPod, I guess — and I'd price one of those Kanga kit rooms. Eighteen-nine for a hundred and twenty square feet is tempting.

DEREK: Careful with that one. The eighteen-nine is a shell — no electrical, no insulation, no floor finish. Their own turnkey program prices the same room north of forty. All three of the finished ones are in my spreadsheet: WorkPod, Studio Home, Modern Shed.

RENEE: Hold the spreadsheet, Derek — I promise we'll use it later. Wendy, who would you call?

WENDY: Whoever my neighbors used — Modern Shed — but only if someone else manages the whole thing. I don't want a summer of phone calls.

TOM: Nobody's said the big-box shed kits, you notice. There's a reason. Those are for lawnmowers.

[00:17] RENEE: Noted. I'm going to show you a concept now. [Concept board displayed.] A factory-built backyard studio, roughly a hundred square feet in the base version. Delivered flat-packed, installed in one day, and at this size there's usually no building permit required. Standard: pre-wired electrical, smart entry lock, floor-to-ceiling dual-pane glass across the front, pitched roof. Options include sound insulation, heating and cooling, and swapping glass panels for solid privacy panels. Before anyone talks — Derek, I'm looking at you with love —

[laughter]

RENEE: — I want five quiet minutes. Sheets are in front of you. Write three things: your first reaction, one thing you love, one thing that worries you. We'll build from what you wrote, not from whoever talks first.

[Five minutes of silent writing.]

[00:24] RENEE: Alicia, read me yours.

ALICIA: I wrote "light." The glass is the whole thing for me — my clients would melt for that light. My worry: my yard faces west. That glass wall in a Fontana August at four p.m.? You'd cook like a rotisserie.

GREG: Nearly word for word what I wrote. Love the look; but I sat in a friend's sunroom last July and it was a greenhouse with furniture. If there's no serious cooling, it's a very pretty oven.

MARISOL: Mine says "privacy." My neighbors' second floor looks straight down into our yard. A glass box means I'm the neighborhood television, and I am not that interesting.

[laughter]

WENDY: I wrote "on display" — same worry. I'd want to choose when it's open and when it's closed off.

RENEE: Marisol, stay there a second. Say more about "choose." What would choosing look like, practically?

MARISOL: Glass when I want to see the garden. Something solid or frosted when I don't. They mentioned swapping in privacy panels — that, or blinds built into the glass. If the glass came with a privacy mode, that solves it completely. All glass, all the time, no.

PRIYA: That option honestly answers both problems at once. The good dual-pane glass handles the heat better, and the privacy piece keeps Mrs. Binoculars out of my video calls.

[laughter]

SAM: Mine was about glare — I stare at color-accurate monitors all day. But it's the same answer: I need to control the light, not eliminate it. A windowless box would be worse. That's just a garage with better marketing.

DEREK: I wrote "what's it made of." Glass is glass, fine — but the walls are the product. If those panels are single-skin steel, everything else is lipstick.

TOM: Mine just says "how much." We'll get there, I assume.

RENEE: [laughing] We will, Tom. Written down and everything.

[00:33] RENEE: Let's stay on comfort. The concept lists heating and cooling as an option, not standard. Reactions?

GREG: That's backwards. It's non-negotiable in the IE summer. It hit 108 in Ontario last July. A backyard room without a mini-split isn't a room — it's seasonal storage.

DEREK: Agreed, and I'll go further — the insulation matters as much as the unit. My buddy's WorkPod ships insulated as standard, he added the mini-split, and his electric bill barely moved. You bolt a mini-split onto a tin can, you're air-conditioning the yard. And while I'm on build quality —

RENEE: Derek, hold that thought — I want it, and I'll come back for it. But I haven't heard Tom on this one. Tom: heating and cooling, option or standard?

TOM: Standard. My wife is not walking out there in January or in August otherwise, and Redlands gets both ends of it. If I'm paying finished-room money, I expect a finished room — insulated, heated, cooled, done.

WENDY: Standard. A fan is not climate control, whatever the brochure says.

SAM: Everyone I know who bought the fans-only version of anything regrets it by August.

PRIYA: If it can't hold seventy-two degrees on a video call in July, it cannot be my office. That's the whole test.

RENEE: Okay — I'm hearing insulation plus real heating and cooling as a floor, not an upgrade. Derek, now the build-quality thought.

DEREK: Just this: ask what the panel is. Insulated composite, you've got a building. Untreated wood kit, you've got a rot timeline. Thin steel, you've got a barbecue. The kit sellers get away with it because the headline price hides what's missing — that Kanga number doubles once the room is actually finished. The finished-unit companies that get this right lead with it.

[00:41] RENEE: Good. Now the inside. This can come as an empty shell or fitted out. What's in your ideal version?

PRIYA: A desk, shelves, and lighting that doesn't make me look like a hostage on video calls. If they sell a work-from-home package, that's the one I buy. I'm done duct-taping flat-pack furniture into an office.

SAM: Same. Fit it out for work and charge me for it — my time is worth more than what I'd save finishing a shell.

ALICIA: Mine's the other package, same logic. The studio version — proper flooring with some give to it, a mirror wall, decent air movement. If it arrives ready for movement classes, that's a business expense I can justify to my accountant.

WENDY: I'd take Alicia's version, honestly — not for clients, for me. Yoga, reading, a room that isn't about anyone else's needs. That's the empty-nest dream, apparently.

TOM: The shell sounds cheaper until you price flooring and shelving separately. I did that math once on a garage conversion. Never again.

RENEE: Greg, you're nodding but you've gone quiet — shell or fitted?

GREG: Fitted. The empty shell is how it becomes the trampoline: a good idea nobody ever finishes.

[laughter]

RENEE: And the guest-room idea — anyone picturing this for visitors?

WENDY: I thought about it for about a minute. No bathroom, no water — so my sister would be trooping across the lawn at two in the morning. It's not a guest room; it's a nicely lit tent.

MARISOL: Agreed. Office or studio, yes. Guest room, not without plumbing — and then you're in Tom's neighbor's world, with the permits and the hundred fifty grand.

[00:48] RENEE: Two more features, quickly, then money. First: the smart entry lock.

SAM: [shrugs] It's fine? It's not why anyone buys this.

PRIYA: A lock is a lock. As long as there is one and it works.

DEREK: I'd rather they put that money into thicker panels, frankly.

RENEE: Polite indifference — got it. Second: power. This one comes pre-wired: outlets, lighting circuit, panel hookup by an electrician on install day. For contrast, some cheaper units out there do solar-only, and the budget shells expect you to run an extension cord.

GREG: An extension cord across the lawn to my office? That's a lawsuit with grass on it.

[laughter]

DEREK: Solar-only sounds green until you try to run a mini-split in August. It can't. Pre-wired is the right call — the WorkPod is honest about this too: one cable, one electrician, done. It's half of why those installs go so smoothly.

MARISOL: Pre-wired, absolutely. Real power, installed by a professional, working on day one. Also — small thing — my HOA will ask about height and setbacks, not about locks. Under the permit line matters more than any gadget.

[00:53] RENEE: All right. Money — and we do this in writing first, exactly as promised. On your sheets: the studio we've been describing all evening, with what this room called the floor — insulated panels, the good glass with a privacy option, real heating and cooling — delivered and installed. Three numbers, your own, nobody else's. First: the price where it starts to feel like a **bargain** — below that, you'd wonder what's wrong with it. Second: the price where it starts **getting expensive** — you'd still consider it, but you'd feel it. Third: the price where it becomes **too expensive to consider**, no matter how nice it is. All three before anyone speaks.

[Writing.]

[00:57] RENEE: Bargain first. Around the room, just the number.

TOM: Six thousand.

GREG: Eight.

WENDY: Eighty-five hundred.

MARISOL: Nine.

SAM: Nine.

PRIYA: Ten.

ALICIA: Ten — if the studio flooring's included.

DEREK: Thirteen.

TOM: Thirteen thousand as a *bargain*, Derek?

DEREK: A finished, insulated building for six grand isn't a bargain, Tom — it's a scam with a roof.

[crosstalk]

RENEE: [laughing] Okay — this is exactly the argument I wanted, and we're having it one voice at a time. Getting-expensive next. Tom, start us.

TOM: Nine.

GREG: Twelve.

WENDY: Twelve-five.

MARISOL: Thirteen.

SAM: Thirteen.

PRIYA: Fourteen.

ALICIA: Fourteen-five.

DEREK: Eighteen.

RENEE: And the third number — too expensive to consider.

TOM: Fourteen. And my wife will negotiate me upward, I'm sure.

[laughter]

GREG: Eighteen.

WENDY: Eighteen.

MARISOL: Nineteen.

SAM: Nineteen.

PRIYA: Twenty.

ALICIA: Twenty-one.

DEREK: Twenty-six.

RENEE: Sam, I'll note for the record that you are the exact middle of this room on all three numbers.

SAM: Story of my life.

[laughter]

[01:04] RENEE: Priya, walk me up your ladder. What's behind the twenty?

PRIYA: I anchored on what I know is out there. The WorkPod is twenty-one grand, basically — advertised, before delivery. So my ceiling is a notch under that. Whoever this new company is, they're not the brand my neighbor already owns. The name isn't worth full freight on day one.

GREG: Same math, honestly. The finished ones run eighteen to twenty-one advertised — and the eighteen-nine kit is a shell, so that number's not real anyway. I started below the finished cluster and worked down.

DEREK: And I'll say it again for the transcript: my three numbers are for *delivered and installed*. Advertised isn't installed. It's the only honest way to write a ladder.

WENDY: I didn't know any prices, so mine was simpler: what number survives a conversation with my husband.

RENEE: A rigorous methodology.

[laughter]

[01:09] RENEE: Last exercise. If this company could get exactly one thing perfect — one — what should it be? Quick answers, around the room.

ALICIA: The glass-with-privacy option. That's the difference between a showpiece and a room I'll actually use at four p.m.

GREG: Climate. Cool in August or nothing else matters.

DEREK: Build quality — insulated panels. Everything else stands on that.

PRIYA: The work package. Sell me a finished office, not a room.

TOM: Price. Come in under the established guys and I'm listening.

WENDY: Privacy. Same as Alicia.

SAM: Climate, then the desk setup.

MARISOL: The privacy glass. We appear to have a theme.

[01:13] RENEE: You've been a fantastic group — even you, Derek.

DEREK: Especially me.

[laughter]

RENEE: Envelopes at the door, and the sponsor thanks you for your evening. Good night, everyone.

[END OF SESSION — 01:14]

groups.context: The silent-writing readout at [00:24] is dominated by this topic — Alicia, Greg, Marisol, Wendy, and Sam all wrote about it — and it takes three of the eight votes in the closing one-thing-perfect round at [01:09].

guides.title: Round 7 — Mining a Transcript for Findings
guides.body:
**Code, then count, then weigh.** First pass: label every recurring idea with a short code (privacy, heat, install speed, price…) — don't analyze yet, just tag. Second pass: count. How many participants raised each idea, and how many brought it up *unprompted*? Third pass: weigh intensity. "Non-negotiable" and a shrug are both one mention; they are not the same finding. Emotion, specificity, and personal stories mark the reactions that will drive real purchase behavior.

**Mentions vs. meaning.** For brand talk, unaided mentions early in a session are the strongest awareness evidence you'll get. But log the *tone* with the tally: a brand named as the standard to beat, a brand the room itself reclassifies into a different product category, and a brand nobody mentions in an hour of category talk are three different competitive facts wearing the same tally mark. When a room sorts a tempting price into "a project, not a purchase," that sorting is a finding about the category line — record it.

**One loud voice is not consensus.** Every group has a dominant talker; a good moderator reins them in — notice when that happens, because it tells you whose airtime to discount. Silent-writing exercises are the antidote: what people wrote before anyone spoke is uncontaminated by the room. Treat written responses as the cleanest data in any session.

**Price talk and anchoring.** Participants who know the category anchor on the advertised prices they've seen — and typically set their ceilings *below* them for an unproven brand. Use the written ladder, take the middle of the distribution rather than the mean on each rung (two outliers can move an average by thousands), and record *why* the outliers sit where they sit — the reasoning is a finding too. Watch for participants who state which completion level their numbers assume; a ladder written for "delivered and installed" and one written for an advertised base price are different instruments.

**Respect the n.** Eight people in one metro generate hypotheses and vocabulary for the survey; they size nothing. Write findings as "this room said," never "the market wants."

**Pointers for this round:** track which brands come up when Renee asks about shopping lists, how each is characterized, and which ones the room re-files into the wrong-category bin; in the feature sections, the silent-writing readout and the closing one-thing-perfect round carry the most weight; and the price-ladder numbers were written before discussion — treat that round as the session's cleanest read, and take medians rung by rung.

resources.title: From Round 4 — Backyard Studios, Space Pods, and Expandable Tiny Homes: A Category Field Guide (condensed)
resources.body: *Structure & Site Quarterly, condensed.* Two products share the backyard, and the legal line between them is the ADU definition: complete independent living facilities — living, sleeping, eating, cooking, sanitation (California Gov. Code § 66313). **Finished studios and pods (no plumbing, often no permit):** the reference product is the **Autonomous WorkPod** — 102 sq ft, advertised at **$20,900** DIY, insulation standard, single-cable power hookup, direct online purchase with published reviews. **Studio Home's Signature Series** (96–192 sq ft, from about **$18,000**) competes on a configurator with installation and interiors priced separately; **Modern Shed** sells consultant-led bespoke studios, quote-only, with California installer support; **Kanga Room Systems'** Modern Kwik Room 10×12 (120 sq ft) is the kit benchmark — **$18,900** as a shell, **$40,600** turnkey in its Texas-only program. **Expandable homes and foldable ADUs (kitchen + bath, ADU-capable):** **Bright Box Homes** from $35,995; **Elite Nest 400** from $16,999 with a "95% complete" claim and thin documentation; **BOXABL's Casita** at ~$60,000 unit-only or ~$150,000 California turnkey; certified travel trailers such as the **ESCAPE Vista Boho** ($57,640) press the category as a mobile substitute. The analyst's rule: buyers cross-shop within a category — a $16,999 expandable dwelling is not a cheap studio.

resources.title: From Round 4 — Backyard-Unit Buyer Trends by Homeowner Segment (condensed)
resources.body: *Home & Yard Business Journal, condensed.* Three buyer segments: the **remote professional** (~45% of purchases) wants a desk-ready office — work surface, shelving, task lighting — and prizes daylight, yet glass-forward units generate the category's top post-purchase complaints: afternoon heat gain and "working on display." Demand has shifted toward dual-pane glazing with a privacy option. The **wellness user** (~30%, fastest-growing) wants resilient or sprung flooring, a mirror wall, and — most of all — privacy. The **guest-space buyer** (~25%, softening) cools off once they learn unplumbed structures can't serve as true guest quarters — the buyers who persist migrate into plumbed, ADU-capable units at two to three times the outlay. Across all segments: climate comfort is now a threshold expectation — insulation plus a mini-split is the minimum for year-round use in hot metros, and fans-only units draw elevated complaints and returns. Buyers don't ask for smart extras, but expect professional day-one power and a locking door.

resources.title: From Round 4 — Opportunities & Forecasts for the Compact-Structure Market (condensed)
resources.body: *Compact Structures Outlook, condensed.* The category is forecast to grow ~11% annually through 2030, led by the finished-studio segment and powered by remote work and permit-light formats. The five attributes buyers will most demand: (1) insulated composite panel construction — the strongest predictor of owner satisfaction; (2) dual-pane glazing with a privacy option; (3) a full climate package (insulation + mini-split HVAC); (4) work-from-home interior fit-out; (5) pre-wired electrical with smart entry lock. Materials warnings: single-skin steel and untreated timber kits are losing share on durability complaints; premium hardwood cladding wins compliments, not orders; unfinished shells disappoint owners who underestimate finishing costs. Pricing outlook: advertised prices for finished 100–120 sq ft studios cluster between $18,000 and $21,000 (WorkPod $20,900; Studio Home from ~$18,000; Kanga $18,900 — for a shell that reprices at $40,600 turnkey). Advertised prices are not comparable across completion levels; the decision metric is total cost to a legally usable, installed space.
